replies.name: Aleksander Lada
replies.text:
I've been experimenting with this idea for a while in this project of mine. I reached a point in which the orchestrator agent was too busy managing worker agents, so I couldn't discuss the project without messing with its context.

So now I have an agent to orchestrate the orchestrators. Works like charm, but now I need two $200 subscriptions 😂

Your chief of staff is my engineer, but I have a project manager above it, which I call an architect. The project used to be called Loom, and the engineer used to be called Weaver, precisely because it's about orchestrating threads.

Anyhow, I've had some issues with Codex's excessive conciseness - it saves tokens but it ends up not passing down the full context. So I use Claude as the architect/engineer and Codex as the worker. It's been wild watching these folks work together!

https://t.co/NmLk9SHBEP

replies.name: Nick
replies.text:
This has fundamentally changed how I use Codex

- everything runs out of a single persistent thread (my "chief of staff")
- anytime I start a new project or workstream, I have that thread spin up a new thread (because it's already found the context from slack, etc)
- the CoS thread checks in on the project threads during heartbeats, and occasionally sends relevant updates from slack to that thread

everything flows naturally to the top
